Future Continuous: Used to express an action continuing at some point in the future time. We shall be singing a song. The girls will be playing football.

Future Perfect: Denotes the action will be completed in the future before another future action takes place. I shall have written my letter before he comes. You will have heard this news already. Nobody will have taken anything from you when you go home this afternoon. I hope you will have washed your face before you come into the room again.

Future Perfect Continuous: An action — whether finished or unfinished, will be in progress for some time. We shall have been playing three hours when you visit here. They will have been making preparation for the marriage for two months.

THE SEQUENCE OF TENSES
A past tense in the main clause is followed by a past tense in the subordinate clause.
She replied that she had no money with her. They found that he was dishonest.
There are two exceptions to this.
When the subordinate clause expresses a universal truth, then it will be in the present tense even if the main clause is in the past tense.
He said that all men are mortal. She said that God is love. He taught us that honesty is the best policy.
If the subordinate clause is introduced by the conjunction ‘than’, even if the main clause is in the past tense, it may be followed by a present tense in the subordinate clause.
She liked him better than she likes you. (Main clause – past tense; subordinate clause – present tense) He helped me more than he helps his own children.
A present or future tense in the main clause may be followed by any tense (present, past or future) required by the sense, in the subordinate clause.

She thinks that she works hard. She thinks that he worked well. She will think that he is present. She works hard lest she should fail. She worked hard lest she should fail. She will work hard lest she should fail.
VOICE
The hunter killed the tiger – Active Voice. The tiger was killed by the hunter – Passive Voice.

In the first sentence, the subject (hunter) is the doer of the action, that is the subject is active. In the second sentence the subject (tiger) is the sufferer or receiver of the action, that is the subject is not active but passive. In the first sentence the verb ‘killed’ is in active voice. In the second sentence the verb ‘was killed’ is in the passive voice.
Simple present: The grocer sells sugar (AV) → Sugar is sold by the grocer (PV). Cats catch mice (AV) → Mice are caught by cats (PV).
Present Continuous: The farmer is tilling the land (AV) → The land is being tilled by the farmer (PV). Are they picking some flowers?
(AV) → Are some flowers being picked by them?
(PV)
Present Perfect: He has written a letter (AV) → A letter has been written by him (PV). I have taken your books (AV) → Your books have been taken by me (PV).
Simple Past: He took my book (AV) → My book was taken by him (PV). Did he tell the truth?
(AV) → Was the truth told by him?
Past Continuous: He was playing football (AV) → Football was being played by him (PV). Were the farmers sowing the seeds?
(AV) → Were the seeds being sown by the farmers?
Past Perfect: The boys had eaten the cake (AV) → The cake had been eaten by the boys (PV).
Simple future: We shall finish the work by 6 p.m. (AV) → The work shall be finished by us by 6 p.m. (PV). He will hurt you (AV) → You will be hurt by him (PV).
Future Perfect: He will have closed the shop by 8 o’clock (AV) → The shop will have been closed by him by 8 o’clock (PV).
Certain verbs take two objects after them in the active voice, and in the passive voice one of the objects becomes the subject and the other is retained as object.
He gave me some apples (AV) → I was given some apples by him (PV). He taught us English (AV) → We were taught English by him (PV).
Some intransitive verbs (verbs that do not have direct objects) are used with prepositions as transitive verbs — have them in the passive voice.
All laughed at her (AV) → She was laughed at by all (PV). She agreed to my proposal (AV) → My proposal was agreed to by her (PV).
Imperative mood (Command or request): Shut the door. → Let the door be shut.
Interrogative (Question sentence): When did you write this letter?
→ When was this letter written by you?
Passive voice without “by”: They elected him as king (AV) → He was elected as king (PV). They named their son Samuel (AV) → Their son was named Samuel (PV).

ADVERB
Adverbs are used to modify verbs.
Kinds of Adverb
Adverb of Manner — wisely, well, fast, bravely, badly and slowly. (Answers the question HOW?)
Adverb of Place — outside, inside, everywhere, anywhere, here, there, hither and thither, forward and backward. (Answers the question WHERE?)
Adverb of Time — today, tomorrow, yesterday, daily, early, presently, immediately and ago. (Answers the question WHEN?)
Adverb of Number — twice, always, often, seldom and once. (Answers the question HOW OFTEN?)
